To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the renal pressure-mediated transgene expression characteristics are different according to the administration routes.
the renal pressure-mediated transgene expression is applicable to renal artery or uretheral injections and the renal pressure method is a safe and useful method for gene delivery to the kidney.
the renal pressure transfection method is a useful tool for gene transfer into rat kidney and the optimal pressure intensity in rat kidney is different according to administration route.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characteristics of gene expression and distribution in the rat kidney after renal arterial and/or ureteral injections using the renal pressure method.
the renal pressure method as an in vivo gene transfer method for kidney.
the development of a kidney-specific gene delivery system and the establishment of a novel gene delivery method using a pressure-mediated gene delivery technique.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the renal pressure-mediated gene delivery method has been proven to be a useful tool for the development of gene therapy for kidney diseases.
the renal pressure-mediated transduction method can be applied to other administration routes and animals, which is an important finding for further clinical applications.

the renal pressure-mediated gene transfer method is effective in both renal arterial and uretered injections, and the optimal pressure intensity is 1.2 and 0.90 N/cm2, respectively, in the rat kidney.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the renal arterial injection is more effective for gene delivery to renal cortex and ureteral injection is more effective to renal medulla.
the renal pressure-mediated transfections are effective for both renal arterial and ureterioral injections in rat kidney.
the renal arterial route is more effective for gene delivery to the cortex, while the ureteral route is more effective in the cortex and medulla.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can control gene transfer efficiency by adjusting the pressure intensity.
we can choose the most appropriate administration routes and pressure intensity to achieve the desired transfection efficiency and distribution of transgene expression in the kidney.

the optimal pressure intensity for each administration route differs and that the transfection efficiency of the renal pressure method is about 100-fold greater than that of the simple injection method.
